answer:
**Separate assumptions for unbiased coefficients from assumptions for conventional uncertainty formulas.** A common Gauss–Markov formulation requires a model linear in parameters, full column rank, zero conditional error mean, and errors with constant variance and no cross-observation correlation conditional on the design. Textbooks group these into different numbered lists, so state the conditions rather than relying only on “five assumptions.” [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

**Heteroscedasticity means unequal error variance.** For example, prediction errors for large firms' revenue may be more variable than for small firms. If the conditional mean model is still correct and errors have zero conditional mean, OLS coefficients can remain unbiased. What fails is the usual constant-variance covariance estimate and the claim that OLS is best among linear unbiased estimators under the original theorem.

**Why p-values can become wrong.** A coefficient estimate divided by an underestimated standard error looks more significant than it should. Heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors address variance-estimation issues under their own large-sample/design conditions; weighted least squares can improve efficiency when the variance structure is suitably modeled.

Normality is not needed for the basic Gauss–Markov best-linear-unbiased result, though it supports particular exact finite-sample inference statements. Robust standard errors do not fix omitted-variable bias, dependence ignored by the covariance method, or a wrong conditional mean. Diagnose those issues separately.

**Technical details and references.**

One standard Gauss–Markov formulation assumes a model linear in parameters, full-rank regressors, zero conditional error mean, constant conditional error variance, and uncorrelated errors. Random sampling is often used to justify the last conditions; textbook lists group assumptions differently. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html) [2](https://www.statlearning.com/)

$$y=X\beta+\epsilon,\quad E[\epsilon\mid X]=0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I.$$

Heteroscedasticity violates constant variance. If exogeneity and rank conditions still hold, OLS coefficients remain unbiased, but ordinary homoscedastic standard errors are wrong and OLS need not be most efficient among linear unbiased estimators. Use heteroscedasticity-robust covariance or a justified variance model. Normal errors are not required for the Gauss–Markov BLUE result; they support additional exact finite-sample inference.
